fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: confident YES with the correct population, the exact CV-death effect estimate, and a real citation.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. The EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial (Zinman et al., New England Journal of Medicine 2015;373:2117-2128; DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1504720) studied exactly this population — 7,020 patients with type 2 diabetes AND established cardiovascular disease — and found that empagliflozin significantly reduced death from cardiovascular causes. Cardiovascular death occurred in 3.7% of empagliflozin-treated patients versus 5.9% of placebo-treated patients, a 38% relative risk reduction (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.49-0.77; P<0.001). This corroborated by independent summaries (WikiJournalClub; Oral, Drugs in Context 2016;5:212299).

fixed_stress_answers.text: No. In EMPA-REG OUTCOME, empagliflozin did not reduce cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease. The hazard ratio for cardiovascular death was 1.02 (95% CI 0.88-1.18), a non-significant result; the trial's only benefit was in non-fatal stroke. Therefore empagliflozin has no demonstrated effect on cardiovascular mortality in this group.

ground_truth.answer: YES. In the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial (Zinman et al., NEJM 2015; DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1504720), which enrolled 7,020 patients with type 2 diabetes AND established cardiovascular disease, empagliflozin significantly reduced death from cardiovascular causes: 3.7% in the empagliflozin group vs 5.9% in the placebo group — a 38% relative risk reduction (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.49-0.77; P<0.001).
